newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Aid workers return to Kabul, but face problems.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers return to Kabul, but face problems.

text.p: Many international aid workers who fled Kabul two weeks ago when the opposition arrived within rocketing range of the city are returning, but they face problems with rules imposed by the Taleban limiting access to women.

"They are coming back to keep their programmes running and because of the fact that (the military situation) seems to be a stalemate and the opposition has not shown a tendency to rocket the city," Ross Everson, of the aid umbrella organisation Agency Coordinating Body for Afghan Relief, said on Thursday.
"...We are all aware that the opposition may come tomorrow and we'll all have to evacuate again."

Some 50 international aid staff left Kabul on July 25, shortly after the opposition advanced to within 12 miles (20 km) of Kabul. The advance was accompanied by a number of opposition air raids on the city.

Everson said that the aid community was still encountering problems with a series of decrees issued by the Taleban's religious police on July 16 limiting contact between international aid agencies and women.
"The decrees are a major problem, the Red Cross and the (United Nations) World Food Programme are carrying on, but many other programmes have been stopped," he said.
The decrees were sent to all aid agencies and hospitals in Kabul.

"The regulations of our Islamic country are based on the non-employment of females in international or local offices, and issuing limits on women's rights to leave their houses is an Islamic obligation that must be observed by foreign and local institutions," the decrees say.
They continue to stipulate that women are only allowed to work in the medical sector and that aid to female recipients should be channelled through their male relatives.

According to a joint letter sent to the Taleban by the aid agencies, the decrees contradict previous agreements between the agencies and the Taleban authorities and, if they are strictly followed, would force them to shut down a number of their programmes.

"The new regulations contradict existing agreements between the Afghan authorities and non-governmental organisations (NGOs). Agreements that have been signed by the Afghan authorities should be honoured. These regulations seriously damage the ability of humanitarian agencies to provide assistance to vulnerable groups, particularly women," says the letter.

"Women and children are frequently the worst victims of war, and aid must be targeted on them. According to the new regulations, women are forbidden to work outside hospitals and clinics. This means that community-based programmes (e.g. nutritional surveys, disease prevention, health education, pre- natal care) cannot continue.

"These new regulations also state that assistance to widows can only be received through male blood relatives and that female surveyors are forbidden. This means that assistance cannot reach those in need," it continues.

The Taleban regulations barring women from working have hit Kabul's huge population of war widows particularly hard. Already marginalised and struggling to make ends meet in Afghanistan's traditionally male-orientated society, the Taleban's formalisation of the ban on working has driven many of Kabul's widows to destitution.
Care International, one of the world's largest aid agencies, felt forced by the new regulations to suspend its widows feeding programme.

"(Our programmes) are temporarily suspended since these regulations make the food distribution operationally impossible, and are an attempt to cause Care to break with its core values," said Stuart Worsley of Care on Wednesday.

"Care does and cannot distinguish between people in need according to gender, race, social status or political standing. For Care to continue to provide assistance to men and not to women would go against our principles," said Worsley.
Worsley believes that the regulations can be modified to make them acceptable to both the Taleban and the aid community.

"We have spoken to several ministries and their response has been both encouraging and understanding. They have shown concern: we believe that they are doing what they can to come to some kind of satisfactory solution," he said.
